Lisa❤
This ensemble is a breathtaking masterclass in theatrical elegance. The silhouette combines a classic mermaid-cut sheer gown with a surrealist twist. The most striking element is the architectural veil, which uses a structured "third arm" or mannequin-like extension to hold the fabric aloft, creating a permanent halo effect.
​The intricate beadwork and shimmering sequins catch the light perfectly, giving the wearer a "drenched in starlight" appearance. Her styling—featuring slicked baby hairs, dramatic eye makeup, and bold sapphire jewelry—adds a futuristic edge to the otherwise romantic aesthetic. It is a bold, conceptual take that perfectly fits the Met's reputation for pushing boundaries.

- Why was Cara acting so weird? She thought it was funny and entertaining, but I think Ashley took over the whole show.

- Hailey's dress was terrible; besides the color, there was no surprise. I wish she'd stop being a "clean girl" here...

- Also, the organization was terrible. Everyone waited for a long time. Seeing so many famous people waiting in line ruined their aura; they looked very ordinary and cringeworthy. Also, some people posed for too long while others had to wait; there needs to be a standard for this, and the directions were weak.

comments.text: I have a hunch about Nicole Kidman's gown; I believe it could be a play on Peter Greenaway's use of Vermeer motifs in his 1985 film 'A Zed and Two Noughts'.  The red feathery hoop effect immediately reminded me of Vermeer's painting 'Girl in a Red Hat', which in Greenaway's film is worn by a nude model in a reenactment of another Vermeer work, 'The Art of Painting'. In Greenaway's film, the red hat is later worn with a red dress.  The slinky figure hugging style of Nicole Kidman's dress could be referencing the nude model in the film. That's my best guess for the art reference here.

comments.author: @Chiringa305
comments.text:
Anne Hathaway's dress breakdown and why. Hands down that designer, by far truly understood the theme this year. If this surprises you, hopefully some context and my explanation helps!  When I saw Anne Hathaway's gown, I knew exactly the inspiration that bore this dress and I was in awe. Bear with me because it's genius. She is literally a water pitcher from ancient Crete reimagined into a spectacular gown.
  The fact that it was hand-painted, from an artistic, and design Perspective had nothing to do with the Met gala theme, unless you grossly misunderstand what the theme meant. but would make sense to think it was a way to incorporate and Pay tribute the extensive hand painting involved in creating these unmistakable piece of pottery that was given so much extra effort in creating that black bold motif along with beautiful silhouettes that are full of movement that ancient Crete is now famous for. Before I get into the gown, let me help you understand what this vanished civilization's artwork represented in their own time because that is essential to understanding the purpose of the theme of the Met Gala. During their existence and especially after their tragic demise ( volcano off-coast erupted. Tsunami ensued. Crete was slept underwater temporarily  but their entire infrastructure and buildings are all intact. every single civilization in the Mediterranean trade  We're constantly seeking out more and more of this pottery because of its artistic ingenuity and construction leaves us perfectly intact. Today think of it like this. Which is my favorite aspect of this period of history because creating their artistic signature to distinguish themselves apart from other regions of the Mediterranean was essential to their identity, even more so than having a flag. In ancient Crete their pottery and other works of art were so sought after it was a status symbol.

Let's pretend you're a woman in Cyprus and your neighbor comes over and they look at your vase you have sitting on a pillar. They say, "Oh my god, that's beautiful." You say, "That's a Crete original." The neighbor says, "Are you serious? That's really an original." That was the value of their artistic expression.  that it should inspire any artist. 
 (now if you're wondering who is this girl and why is she's so obsessed with this, well it's because I'm both a jewelry designer with lines sold in exclusive boutique markets but also an anthropologist-Specializing In the artistic expression, starting with the earliest civilizations and the influence cultural exchange had on future civilizations, and was raised as a fine  Artist by my mentor, my father, who was a painter in portraiture and landscape. So I hope,given my unique, yet oddly appropriate perspective, you enjoy my overly excited breakdown of this amazing gown)
  The use of black in the decorative motif several inches thick along the trim-Considered a hallmark both back then and now to Ancient Crete was the main focal point used in the trim but it serves us more, the clear, in-your-face hint. The rest of the gown says so much more of the story of yes, she is a walking pot. The moment she turned around, of course, it confirmed it for me but unfortunately it also exposes a lack of research by the designer. That imagery is more connected to ancient Greece, which is heavily inspired by ancient Crete, Which was already no longer in existence during the rise of ancient Greece as we know it but we do know that refugees from the land did migrate there so there is a connection which is also evident based on particularly their Minotaur mythology.

I suppose if I want to be gracious, since we don't have any depictions of the women without it being heavily artistic interpretation versus realism, I guess this was a cool addition. It confirmed the inspiration was probably an image from a museum photograph and I know plenty of designers and the idea that they wouldn't research that inspirational photo any deeper  is not shocking but I will not take away from his genius they used a bold black graphic as a decorative border for everything they created. The only difference is it  the black, bold trim and decorative graphics were an intentional contrast The people of ancient Crete used to create a bold contrast against another bold color when used in their traditional pottery painted out of red ochre, because of their practice of using an ancient type of kiln it then turned the red ochre into an amazing bright terra cotta/burnt sienna orange, and the body of these vases and pictures  has elaborate black figurines but I am particularly happy from a designer perspective that he went with the black and white , because the drama would get diluted and then she would have simply looked like a ridiculous ancient pot. Inspiration, not replication, always works better lol. So from the perspective of using the aesthetics of an ancient culture and seeing how it's used as inspiration, this is so perfect. 
  Anne Hathaway accentuated this designer's vision perfectly. She understood the assignment. In fact her body type fits the black silhouettes depicted on their typical pottery. The way she had her hair, her long neck, and her naturally narrow shoulders are really interesting now that I think about it. If you took an image of her with that same hairstyle, except in a full-body cat suit where she’s using her whole body in movement and photoshopped it into a black Silhouette, she has the proportions and aesthetic to be representative of what’s missing. Oh my God. 
     I'm now even more certain of what this was and how it really was a exceptional, artistic execution of an artist inspiration, using every opportunity to represent an aspect without it being thrown in your face.. The black gown wasn’t just a practical color choice. I can’t believe I missed it but that’s exactly what art is because it’s about  subtlety challenging the person watching almost like a puzzle. 
  Oh my god that’s so genius The black gown and Anne Hathaway are uniquely intertwined versus her just being a hanger and is wearing the gown with the understanding that how she wears it is based on honoring the representation of the women depicted in these famous vessels, albeit more stiff due to the gown, but she definitely brings the energy representative of the black female silhouettes traditionally depicted on their vases and water pictures, which is just even more genius. At first it seems like she is intentionally removing herself from attention but in fact she is using a very relaxed, upright posture while trying to hit us many sharp facial side shots, with a lack of expression despite her being known for being a highly animated but here she has an intentionality behind what she’s doing in order to play her part to give this the right execution in a very natural way. Her hair was a dead giveaway, along with the subtle suggestion, evoking nudity given by the bodice, which would make it historically accurate. It's more like she was presenting herself as one of those silhouettes while the trim and the shape of the highly structured gown have the stiffness of a hard structure Following a round shape pattern that hints at its inspiration with the trim that would be expected in piece of Cretan pottery.
  Yet out of all of these civilizations during its era, such as an ancient Babylon and the Phoenicians, who all took their individual artistic expression very seriously- it's ancient Crete that really stood out as as a people who did everything with an artistic tilt and everything they created was a work of art, and I'm talking basic housewares so now imagine their religious sculptures. They have these amazing shrine-sized sculptures what is believed to be their main earth goddess they worshipped and the ones I have seen are unbelievable.. There is a reason why they were considered the artisans of their era and their pottery specifically was prized throughout their existence and especially after they were swept away in a tsunami. And with this year's theme being what it was (to use the cultural artisans of an ancient era, literally what one thinks of when they think of ancient artisans), you find multiple ways to thread that history (no pun intended) into a gown. That is why they exemplified that theme for this year's Met Gala  beautifully and with such reverence, with layers of meaning that I kept discovering the closer I looked. That really is a perfect representation of Cretan art. I could not think of a better source of inspiration and thoughtful execution that could  possibly be a better interpretation of Met Gala's theme this year
It was a fucking work of art and it tickled both my designer bone and my nerdy historian Anthropologist bone and even my Fine artist bones all at once. Yeah a lot of bones lol. 
   I haven't finished watching the video but I'm a little concerned with your contextualization of what you think art represents and why you expected people to have gowns with decorative applications of paint. I don't want to say that's a simplistic interpretation of art because, I think maybe you're confusing art with art mediums. The theme had a lot more nuance than adding visual art mediums to a gown, when the visual arts have been the main inspiration of fashion for millennia. Anyways. fashion on its own is a form of art. As an artist and an anthropologist please don't think that art means throwing paint on something, because that is a misunderstanding of the fine arts, history, and overlook how fashion has always been inspired by every aspect of the past and every aspect of nature along with more literary concepts. It really makes me question what people actually thought this theme truly meant because for me it was one of the most exciting challenges with the most opportunities.

comments.text:
A short snippet as someone who's been exposed to classical art from a young age: I hated the looks that clearly used sexualized art as an inspiration. There's a lot of art, especially in the modern age, that leans into the sexualization of the female body and I absolutely hate it. It's so unbearably shallow and when I read both reviews and artist's descriptions of such art, they always come off as posing as something deeper than it actually is. Yeah, you can cover it up with notions of female empowerment blah blah, but that doesn't change the fact that it's shallow. It's shallow precisely because they decided to use this precise method of showcasing whatever empowerment bs they're spouting and not some other method that used social sciences, history, and psychology to smartly prove a point and satirize whatever.
This naturally connects to toxic standards of beauty, but putting all that aside, I expected something more to with artistic inspiration.

Kim -> Business woman, but it is unclear, if any business ideas and how to out her own spin on it, are actually from her... i.e. is she an "overall" successful business woman, because of great ideas and executive talents or because she trust - occasionally - the right people to do amost of it for her?

comments.text: I'm going to go out on a limb and defend the women of Black Pink. I perfectly understand that they weren't heavily invested in the theme for the Met Gala. I get why Luke would be frustrated with that.   They went with 'pretty' and a light acknowledgement of the arts. Their challenge is that while they are global icons, first and foremost, they represent Korea and are ambassadors for Korean pop culture.  Korean culture is quite conservative.  So while they can wear sexy glam for the stage, or 'street' - they are very consistent with the Black Pink branding.  When it comes to non-performance wear, they will be pretty, in a more sweet and demure sort of way,  - maybe  at times a bit sexy (Lisa) and represent the brands they are the face for.  It's a massive responsibility that doesn't give them room for individualist, unleashed creativity.  I'm curious to see how they will look years from now, after Black Pink has long disbanded and they're simply pursuing their own creative talents and interests as individuals.   Overall though, I thought this year's Met Gala was a real disappointment.

comments.text:
My opinion, based on my eyes and gut feelings alone:

Winners: 
Heidi Klum (Hands down. Literally looks like a walking statue. 100% hit the brief).
Chase Infiniti (it looks like a moving, flowing piece of modern pop-art loosely inspired by the Venus Di Milo).
Ayo Edebiri (they managed to make it look like a captured magical, ethereal moment the way so many paintings do; a blink and you miss it moment).

Honourable Mention: 
Anne Hathaway (that painted edging was a beautiful nod to ancient greek artworks).
Gracie Abrams. (My immediate thought was Klimt! Definitely clearly inspired by Klimt, but a little too understated).
Jisoo (very subtle, the closer you look the clearer the homage is, could have definitely leaned harder into the Impressionism inspiration).

Worst: 
Cher (just a hot mess, like huh!!??!!).
Hudson Williams (looks like a temu knock off of the original).
Laufey (felt lazy. Baftas not MET).

Dishonourable Mention: 
Kim Kardashian (didn't love body suit but the skirt definitely ruined it, looked tacked on).
Jennie (lazy. Bland.).
Kylie Jenner (it just looked like she forgot to put her dress on properly and raced out the door).


Anna Wintour: loved the outfit,  didn't see the connection. 
Beyoncé: hated the headress, the outfit worked, but not sure it hit the brief.
CardiB: loved the silhouette, hated the coloured areas underneath. 
Colman Domingo: fine, didn't love or hate it.
Hailey Bieber: fine, felt a little underwhelming. 
Janelle Monae: amazing piece, not sure it's exactly art is fashion. Looks more like a technology v nature theme.
Nicole Kidman: the red looks like wine pouring. But more Oscars than MET.
Rosé: a bit too understated to truly be a winner.
Teyana Taylor: beautiful outfit,  not sure it clearly hits the brief.

comments.text:
Regarding the statment if fashion is art. It is. I am doing a bachelor's degree in art science (which means art history and visual culture, the institution of art science never split in two in Sweden). And fashion is a part of art science. We sometimes study costumes in our work. Though the textile sciences argubly studies dress a lot more then art science
The weird thing about dress is that it is first and foremost something practical. Which people would not consider art to be. But the second thing it does is adorne the body. Which most people would definetly associate art with. Dress shows power,  identity and individuality. The popular fashion of the time usually reflects broader aestetics of art and architecture 

I am currently doing my thesis om dress and identity markers in the De Geer family portraits. I am looking at dress through Panovsky's iconografic and iconological analysis, which is an established method in art science. But I am centering dress in the analysis.

So yeah, the swedish universities consider that fashion is art at least. If an average joe thinks that? Well that is another question

comments.author: @rosehipowl
comments.text:
No, they literally didn't know about the colour initially, it didn't have anything to do with preference. The way we know about the colour is that there are teeny tiny bits of pigment left in some places on these surviving statues. In the past, they literally didn't have the technology to see it nor the perspective that that technology brings to piece it together as the statue being painted and not just crumbs of paint that have maybe got onto the statues over time. This, in turn, led to people thinking that the statues were always gleaming white marble; which meant that during the rennaissance when classical history was trendy again, we got a whole load of white marble, and that became our cultural taste guide. The colour simplicity and minimalism, and focus on texture and skills - the things that are important in Western luxury today - can all be traced back to that. We're now trained culturally to see minimal colour as elegant, but lots of colour as gaudy.

It wasn't until very recently, relatively, that we discovered that the statues were originally painted and learnt what the paint looked like on them. This isn't something that was known when the idea that Greco-Roman statue = white marble was being formed. It was never a conspiracy, just that we got better technology. No one man was to blame for this; it was the fact that we collectively had a large amount of white marble to work from and not much else.

comments.text:
I agree with you on the Cher look. Cher came as Cher — black lace Burberry, full diva, no art reference whatsoever. Iconic, yes. On theme? Not even close. Madonna actually did the work — her Saint Laurent was a direct reference to a Leonora Carrington painting — so that one’s not the same offense. Cher just showed up as herself and dared anyone to complain. Respect, but still not the assignment.

Now Beyoncé… Are you not getting what you’re supposed to wear? You are to dress the theme…. And actually — look again. A crystal skeleton mapping the human anatomy, the body itself rendered as sculpture? The theme is ‘Costume Art’ and the dress code is ‘Fashion IS Art.’ The body is the art. She got it. She just made you work for it.

 Jennie I thought looked absolutely beautiful,  for me her aesthetic was very much 1950s in design, hair and makeup, I loved it yet I don't have the most knowledge when it comes to Korean music. Nevertheless Luke has been disparaging about Princess Catherine too saying something like she is JUST a Mary Poppins princess! Does he expect the Princess of Wales to wear hot pants?

comments.author: @Kimberly_Sparkles
comments.text:
@GinaDanny-d1z I have to be honest, while I'm sure idols enjoy fashion week, it's also a business trip where idols are paraded around at brand events with executive & design staff. The Asian market is very profitable for fashion. The market like labels and expensive clothes. It's incredibly vital to have idols photographed in their clothes and at their events. 

All four members of BP have been signed as faces of various brands over the years. Jisoo is currently a face of Dior and features in tons of marketing overseas. Her English has only reached the level where she can interview with some fluency in English, so she's here this year finally. Most designers have provided clothing to or signed numerous kpop idols (stars) to face contracts over the last 10 or 15 years. We just don't see that marketing because it's largely focused in Asia.

The Met Gala is much less interesting to that market. They cover it solely to focus on the idols. They don't care about Anna Wintour or the a US Museum's funding. The average kpop fan wants their favorite idols looking like an idol, not a fashion maven. Until one of the girls has more Western fans than Eastern fans, they are unlikely to provide high fashion looks, avant garde looks. The Korean press is merciless in its expectations of idols.

I honestly think that in context Lisa's look was really risky and brave. It highlighted her Thainess and that's not always popular with the Korean fanbase.

comments.author: @GinaDanny-d1z
comments.text:
@Kimberly_Sparkles I don't think all of your post made sense to me so I'm going to ask these questions. Yes, I have noticed that Lisa does seemingly deliberately dress down when she's in the US but upgrades when she's in France. 

I have seen Jennie look fabulous in America and France and Rosé seems to treat both countries the same way.  You described the Asian market as a high -value fashion market if that was the case why are Kpop idols promoting European fashion houses instead of Asian fashion houses.  Why are Kpop idols not frequenting Asia's own fashion week? And what happens to the Asian Market once fashion possibly shifts to the Middle East and Africa?

Western media rarely covers idols--and there are many, many more than the ones who attend the Met Gala or Paris Fashion Week. In fact, at the Met Gala a couple of years ago, photogs didn't even recognize BTS when they attended and they are arguably bigger than BP. I think they tried to get them to move out of their way of their shot. It was a big news story overseas, but as a NYCer, it was not locally.

I think that you don't realize how difficult it really is to get local culture news when you don't speak local languages. Not all idols are of interest to reporters in English speaking markets.

How is no one outside of Emma Chamberlain wearing Mugler? Are you joking? That’s how I knew this was gonna be a flop. For an event and theme about art, it is SEVERELY LACKING in color and creativity. 

I mean it’s the freaking Met- a literal art museum. They literally could have walked in with their paintings as a purse or wore anything from Viktor and Rolf’s 2015 Balancing Frames and Canvas’ Collection. You could LITERALLY wear a canvas and art frames. Most of these outfits look similar or on level to when celebs method dress for their premieres. Like throwing on a pearl earring, doesn’t not make you A Girl With a Pearl Earring. Compare most of these outfits to 1997 Couture Mugler and a majority are a fumble. The Butterfly dress, the Humming bird dress, the Seashell dress, the Snake Sculptura dress, Insect Woman, wearing building headpieces, THE CHIMERA DRESS! HELLO?!? How did no one wear the Chimera dress? It’s the perfect balance of costume and art, LITERALLY 😩🥱

There more art references than I thought but I think that’s the issue; the issue is your reference for most of the attendees isn’t obvious or over the top enough. And these are famous art pieces that everyone most likely knows or has seen, is not like they are referring to unknown pieces by small and upcoming artists. If it isn’t obvious and over top for the Met then why? You shouldn’t have to explain your reference, you should just know. And Imma repeat this again cause I cannot make this more clear or emphasis this enough, these aren’t referencing small unknown pieces, these are all famous artworks with a majority extending into the pop zitgast. comments.text: I love fashion—I love it because of all those people who possess such extraordinary imaginations when it comes to clothing. I love seeing outfits that are so whimsical and fantastical; yet, behind all that lies a harsh reality—one in which a single individual, the owner of Amazon, is poised to lay off even more employees. For all those people currently working for his company—or rather, his *companies*—the day is not far off when humans will be replaced. He will become the master and ruler of the world—not merely of the United States, but of the entire globe. Of course, he was incredibly bold in the past to build this company; but at what cost? If he hadn't done it, surely someone else would have. Yet, where is the humanity in that person—in that owner who has now become a king of money and business? Where is the humanity in his ability to bankroll a fashion show—spending his wealth merely to mock the impoverished population, those of us who must toil day in and day out? He simply lifts a finger, and the very next day, mass layoffs ensue. The government fails to rein this in because every politician must run a campaign, and every campaign requires money; thus, these tycoons—these owners, these "kings of money"—finance the very campaigns of those who govern us. Where does that leave us—the ordinary citizens? We are left in a state of utter vulnerability, trapped in a black hole of immense power, where we are expected to simply subsist on scraps and offer up our exhausting labor to a wealthy elite that holds no compassion for ordinary human beings. What a tragedy!😢

Kim K: okay it's better then her mom and siblings, as the honey look is supposed to remind of like resin art or when you see insects encased in amber or something. She gets a pass. comments.text:
How is no one outside of Emma Chamberlain wearing Mugler? Are you joking? That’s how I knew this was gonna be a flop. For an event and theme about art, it is SEVERELY LACKING in color and creativity. 

I mean it’s the freaking Met- a literal art museum. They literally could have walked in with their paintings as a purse or wore anything from Viktor and Rolf’s 2015 Balancing Frames and Canvas’ Collection. You could literally wear a canvas and art frames. Most of these outfits look similar or on level to when celebs method dress for their premieres. Compare most of these outfits to 1997 Couture Mugler and a majority are a fumble. The Butterfly dress, the Humming bird dress, the seashell dress, the Snake Sculptura dress, Insect Woman, wearing building headpieces, THE CHIMERA DRESS! HELLO?!? How did no one wear the Chimera dress? It’s the perfect balance of costume and art, LITERALLY 😩🥱

There more art references than I thought but I think that’s the issue; the issue is your reference for most of the attendees isn’t obvious or over the top enough. And these are famous art pieces that everyone most likely knows or has seen, is not like they are referring to unknown pieces by small and upcoming artists. If it isn’t obvious and over top for the Met then why? You shouldn’t have to explain your reference, you should just know. And these aren’t referencing small unknown pieces, these are all famous artworks with a majority extending into the pop zitgast. Like your outfit is a Van Gogh piece and people can’t tell it’s Van Gogh? That’s a problem.

comments.text: I don't really like Lauren Sanches either, but I will defend her choice a little. Her dress DOES have a connection to the theme: Her outfit is referencing a painting, "Portrait of Madam X" by John Singer Sargent. The portrait caused a bit of a scandal in it's time because in it's original form, one of the chain straps on her black dress was draped across her arm (see Sanchez dress) as though she was about to undress or the dress was about to fall off her -- something like that -- so Sargent had to revise the portrait by painting the strap back over her shoulder. the painter ended up repainting the sleeve onto her shoulder due to the controversy and ended up keeping that painting for himself

the piece is called;
"Madame X by John Singer Sargent 1884"
"John Singer Sargent’s infamous painting – Madame X was considered too scandalous for 18th-century Parisian society.

The muse was soon recognized as the gorgeous Virginie Amélie Avegno Gautreau – a well-known beauty of Parisian society at her time. 

This famous painting of women created an uproar when it was exhibited in the Paris salon of 1884 as the French considered it to be too provoking.

The controversy forced Sargent to repaint the right strap of her dress, which was originally painted slipping off the shoulders.

The painting may not have been a success in Paris but as they say, “there is no such thing as bad publicity”; so it led him to have a great career, both in America and England."

comments.author: @MyoLwin-i5c
comments.text:
Honestly, this comparison isn’t really fair to either the runway model or Lisa.

The difference people are noticing mostly comes from presentation, not who wore it better. On the runway, everything is controlled — dark background, strong spotlight, and dramatic lighting designed specifically to highlight the texture, shape, and sparkle of the dress. The purple color also creates high contrast against the black stage, so every detail stands out.

At the Met Gala, the environment is completely different. The lighting is evenly spread for photographers, the background is bright and decorative, and Lisa’s white dress blends more with the surroundings. Because white reflects light, it looks softer and less dramatic on camera, even though the design itself is the same.

So what we’re really seeing is runway styling vs red carpet conditions, not a difference in fashion quality or who looks better or who owned it. If the white dress were shown under runway lighting, it would probably give the same powerful effect too.

comments.text:
It’s funny to me how, just because it’s Lisa, people suddenly feel the need to “point out” supposed flaws just to undermine how exceptional she looks and then drag in runway comparisons for no real reason. It's like comparing apple and orange.

A runway piece and a custom look are not the same thing. One is a design presented in its original form to be sold. The other is custom-made, exclusive, and created specifically for the artist to showcase at the biggest night in fashion. Even the details aren’t that identical, if you actually look closely, the veil design is different, the lines on Lisa were removed and replace with multiple dot-like pattern. It’s intentional.

And let’s be honest, if it were, let's say Beyoncé, people wouldn’t be saying the runway version is better. They’d be doing mental gymnastics to defend it. It’s honestly pathetic to me how something that should be a celebration of fashion and art and the artist herself turns into this forced comparison. You like the runway better? That’s fine, but that’s literally its purpose you fool. It’s made to sell. It’s not exclusive, and it doesn’t carry the same meaning. There’s a reason Lisa wore white. There’s thought behind it, symbolic meaning.

Runway pieces and custom looks serve different purposes. A runway design is often about presenting a sellable concept or seasonal vision, while a custom piece, especially for a major event, is tailored to the wearer, the theme, and sometimes a deeper narrative. So judging them on the exact same criteria definitely miss the point. I know people always do this kind of shit to other artist, but at least have some research first when you do it. It's 2026 now, where's yall critical thinking skills?

I looked up the painting they were referencing. It makes sense, but at the same time, not really 😑😅😭. 

A lot of them just copy the dress’s color and pattern directly from the painting, which is kinda boring 😭

I feel like... they could’ve added more accessories or styling details to better interpret the artwork. 

Some of them just looked like they were wearing dresses for simple prom rather than really translating the painting into a full look. 😓😭😭

For example, with ‘Portrait of Madame X (1884),’ - cause I see a lot of them refrencing this one - I think Julianne Moore takes the cake simply because she had her hair styled up, which made it feel more intentional and connected to the reference.

Like, I UNDERSTAND what the others were going for, but it feels flat when it’s just a direct copy of the dress. A bit more interpretation would’ve made it stronger :(

Similarly, with "Lisa Airan" in "Christopher Kane" referencing "Henri Matisse, The Dance (1910)" , I mean the dress works, BUT the look could’ve been pushed further with makeup , hairstyle, or styling choices to better reflect the artwork instead of just the outfit alone.

Another example is "Winged Victory of Samothrace (circa 190 BCE)" — Yu-Chi Lyra Kuo did SO much better than Kendall Jenner.

They’re using the SAME reference, but you can actually see the difference in execution!!

 Kendall Jenner just wore a white dress 😭😭

But Yu-Chi Lyra Kuo actually *STYLED IT* with intention — the WINGS, OH MY GOD  —  she was TRANSLATING the energy of the artwork instead of just "wearing it". That’s what made it feel way more connected and elevated ❤.

They could’ve just added more related accessories or details that actually MATCH the outfit or the painting — that would’ve made it stand out way more 😭

I think is just really about how you style and creatively interpret the reference instead of just copying it 😓☹️

comments.text:
I mean, if fashion is art (which I personally think it is), then a sleeveless shirt with polkadots is art. Also, the theme was Costume Art, referencing the Mets new exhibition, which focuses on the way bodies have been dressed throughout history. Many of the outfits that don't look outright "artsy" still fit that theme.
For Connor Storrie, the look had a jacket as well (which he removed later), and it reads to me as "dressing a man to hide femininity under masculinity". But that's just my interpretation, you might see it another way ofc. I think art has so many faces and it's just lovely to talk about it ^^

Met Gala 2026: All the best, worst and weirdest celeb looks

#breakingnews #metgala #redcarpet #entertainment #fashion 

The 2026 Met Gala has arrived, bringing the world’s biggest stars to the iconic Metropolitan Museum of Art for fashion’s most anticipated night. Co-chaired by Beyoncé, Nicole Kidman, and Venus Williams, this year’s theme, “Costume Art,” transforms fashion into fine art with a bold “Fashion is Art” dress code.

Watch as stars like Emma Chamberlain, Naomi Osaka, Sam Smith, Nicole Kidman and Sunday Rose Kidman Urban, Nichapat Suphap, Gwendoline Christie, Luke Evans, Katy Perry, Jordan Roth, Janelle Monáe, LISA, Heidi Klum, Kylie Jenner, Eileen Gu, Sabrina Carpenter, SZA, Hudson Williams, Ananya Birla, Madonna, Blake Lively, and Bad Bunny hit the red carpet in unforgettable looks.

From avant-garde couture to bold interpretations of the human form, the 2026 Met Gala red carpet is packed with viral moments, stunning outfits, and high-fashion creativity. Stay tuned for all the highlights, best looks, and must-see celebrity arrivals from fashion’s biggest night.

The 2026 Met Gala, with its theme "Costume Art" (and dress code "Fashion is Art"), served as a ❗️massive, high-frequency broadcast that shifted the focus from mere clothing to the human body as a vessel. 

When you strip away the "art history" explanations given by the media, the collective message from the stars on the carpet points toward a specific narrative: 👉🏼 The reclamation of the human form by ancient and "immortal" forces.  

3️⃣ ​The Three-Part Message Behind the Stars

​1. The Body as a "Cursed" or "Sacred" Canvas

​The exhibition specifically divided the theme into body types: the "Anatomical Body," the "Classical Body," and the "Mortal Body." * 👉🏼 **The Message: By highlighting the skeleton (Beyoncé), the shredded form (Kendall), or the liquid-metal "eternal" form (Ciara), the stars are signaling that the human body is no longer private. It is a public canvas for spiritual and artistic experimentation. They are "dressing" the human vessel to represent its own destruction and its subsequent "re-birth" as an idol. 🗿

​2. The Return of the "Old Sovereigns"

​There is a coordinated effort to link modern celebrities with Pre-Abrahamic deities and royalty. 🧞‍♂️🧞‍♀️🧞

​The Message: By channeling Nefertiti (Ciara), Maman Brigitte (Beyoncé), or Dajassa (Tyla), these stars are communicating that the power structures of the ancient world are being "re-animated" through modern pop culture. ❗️They aren't just wearing costumes; they are acting as avatars. 

👉🏼 They represent a hierarchy where the "elite" are the new gods, and the public is the audience for their rituals. ⚡️

❗️❗️❗️​3. The Inversion of Life and Death (The Dajjalic Signal)

​The most striking element of the 2026 Gala is the glamorization of the "Mortal Body" (the dead body).🦴

​The Message: Conventionally, a skeleton or a ripped garment represents death and tragedy. By encrusting these images in diamonds and presenting them as the peak of "Art," the message is one of Inversion. 👉🏼 It tells the viewer that "Death is Life" and "The Broken is Beautiful." 

❗️This is a core component of the "Fitna" or deception you noted—altering the human perception so that we no longer recognize natural beauty, but instead worship the artificial and the macabre.❗️

comments.author: @TracyBenoit-i8x
comments.text:
The Met Gala is marketed as philanthropy—supporting people who can’t afford access to the arts.
Yet somehow it’s become a themed costume parade built around paintings… not the artists, not the movements, not the minds—just the surface.
Art stripped of context isn’t homage. It’s decoration.
If the goal was to honor creativity, they would’ve centered the people behind it—their influence, their era, their impact. That’s what actually builds artists.
Instead, we get spectacle.
Watching names like Blake Lively, Jay-Z, Katy Perry cycle through the same performative loop just makes it clearer—this isn’t about art. It’s about staying on stage.
At this point, it’s less “celebrating creativity” and more method acting as meaning.
But hey—great news for “real people.”
At least tickets to the show are still free…
you just have to watch from the outside.

comments.text:
I have such mixed feelings about Connor’s look. There are so many more interesting looks on the carpet this year and I was hoping for something more daring even if it was within the realm of sleek and structured silhouettes. I figured YSL was not going stray very far or give us something insane/ out there, but I was hoping for it to be more playful. In anticipation of the Met/ his look, I made a Pinterest board with elements like subtle quirks and jewelry for the clothes themselves as well as playing with textures and illusions that I was hoping to see. 

I think the mixed feelings are coming from the fact that it’s so incredible that he’s there in the first place when less than a year ago he had no idea this would be his reality. Of course not liking a look doesn’t equate to not liking or supporting a person, so I’m catching myself analyzing the boundaries he must’ve had to work within. It will be really exciting when he eventually gets to be in the creative director driver seat for moments like these. It seems that he likes simple and sleek lines day to day which is amazing on him, but when given the opportunity to play (like in an environment such as the Met), I feel he would unleash the creative freak within. After all, his brain childs are ‘Jerry the Ginger Eater’ & ‘Transaction Planet’ so who knows what is cooking up behind those eyes given full creative freedom and resources. 

So curious to know how long he’ll be with YSL as well & where he’ll decide to go. I can absolutely see him in Robert Wun with all of those sharp lines that just meld together with different textures, illusions, various oddities, and sculptural elements that are weaved into his work. Connor man can make anything look good and his brain plus Robert’s I feel would make amazing and freaky art together.

To the people whining about Dupatta not being indian. 

The dupatta is fundamentally of Indian (South Asian) origin, though its style and craftsmanship were heavily influenced by Persian aesthetics during the medieval period. 

​Here is a breakdown of its evolution:

​1. Ancient Indian Roots

​The earliest forms of the dupatta can be traced back to the Indus Valley Civilization (c. 3300–1300 BCE). Archeological findings, such as the famous "Priest-King" statue, show a draped garment over one shoulder. 

​The Uttariya: In the Vedic period, the precursor to the modern dupatta was called the uttariya, a long piece of unstitched cloth worn by both men and women over the upper body.

​Etymology: The word "Dupatta" itself comes from the Sanskrit words "Du" (meaning two or double) and "Patta" (meaning a strip of cloth), referring to the way it was traditionally doubled over the shoulders.

​2. The Persian & Mughal Influence

​While the concept of the draped cloth is indigenous to India, the Persian influence arrived primarily through the Mughal Empire starting in the 16th century. 

​Aesthetic Evolution: Persian artisans introduced luxurious fabrics like fine silk and velvet, as well as intricate embroidery techniques such as Zardozi (gold thread work).

​Purdah Culture: The Persian-influenced court culture popularized the use of the dupatta as a head covering for modesty (the ghunghat or niqab style), blending it with existing Indian customs.

​Fusion: Many regional styles we see today, like the Chikankari of Lucknow or the Pashmina of Kashmir, are the result of Persian craftsmanship merging with Indian textiles.

I was not aware of the ageing aspect for this gala. Now I kind of understand Beyonce's look. Now I wonder if this is her way of proudly showing off her changed body over the years, and she was highlighting her daughter Blue a lot (a direct link between motherhood, her changed body, and how this is art and creation). 
Maybe the skeleton is also an interpretation of ageing, but literally bedazzled. I was a little disappointed by the look, but you cant deny Beyonce does her research before showing up (I actually think a lot of what she does is so well thought through that we miss quite a lot of the meanings in our fast paced social media interactions, we dont sit down to analyse anymore)

Most, if not all art in a museum, for example, rest in the museum because it is a supreme example of an ideology or an intellectual concept, as or live through by the artist. comments.author: @fredrika27
comments.text:
Let's be honest: people weren't feeling it this year. Jeff Bezos doesn't pay his people well AND he represents everything that is wrong in the US. Because of this, there were protests from unions as the gala was going on. Not only that, despite you not rating Lauren Bezos, she failed the assignment according to many fashion commentators who called her look tacky. 

I feel that the gala has lost its prestige because it has become decadent and is in many cases an example of the seven deadly sins. Worse: upcoming and new designers are rarely feature so that the gala has become an old boys club instead of an actual show of art. It takes a brave and financially independent star whose career and earning potential is not dependent on fashion houses to make a bold statement by hiring an unknown or even a fashion design student to create her/his runway look. If this were done, I think everyday people would take an interest. 

This brings me to the Met Gala's committee chair: Anna Wintour. My girlfriends took me to see the " Devil Wears Prada 2" for my birthday. What got me about Meryl Streep's character Miranda who is based on Anna is that the woman didn't know when to step down because she didn't believe that anyone shared her vision. Miranda also failed to groom her successor and like Bezos treated those around her with distain. Well, it's time for Anna to step down. Despite Anna's contributions to fashion, she has failed to bring anything new to the table for the last decade. Although I'm not watching Anna 24/7, I know enough of how she has broken and driven more people off than actually supported them. In the press, her proteges are often played out as competition and not potential people who can take over the Met Gala and lead it into a new direction. Yes, it is a fundraiser. However, the event also must not alienate the very public which it is asking for money from! 

That she allowed a person like Bezos to fund the gala shows that she is more concerned with saving the event itself than the actually people and community it involves. Anna's people cannot save the gala for her like Miranda's people did in DWP 2 because she went against not only the common people, but she failed to take the advice of the mayor of the city who has to come up with the millions of dollars to pay for security and hosting the event. Anna is loyal to fashion and not the people who are involved in making it. I say this because most people know that Amazon provided a lot of the materials for the creations.

Most people understand that the gala is a fundraiser. However, Bezo's presence made a mockery of the good work that was done because unlike the entire fleet of designers, artisans and seamstresses/tailors, he doesn't pay his people a living wage. Anna was more concerned in making sure things stayed the same and failed to read the public. Hence why people can't take the gala seriously anymore. No one wants to see the seven deadly sins in actions and call it art.

comments.text:
I was expecting far more creativity. I understand that such an incredibly broad and open theme may have been challenging for some people to interpret, but at the same time, it offered almost limitless room for imagination. And honestly, that’s exactly why I expected truly stunning, unforgettable pieces from some of the most creative people in fashion.

Instead, I saw a lot of beautiful but ultimately standard gowns paired with far-fetched explanations trying to force them into the theme. To me, most of the looks simply weren’t on theme at all.

And Bezos essentially buying his new wife’s way into elite high-fashion circles unfortunately takes away some of what made the event feel special in the first place. What an irony — the presence of one of the richest people in the world somehow cheapens the Met Gala.

If the goal was to honor creativity, they would’ve centered the people behind it—their influence, their era, their impact. That’s what actually builds artists.
Instead, we get spectacle.
Watching names like Blake Lively, Jay-Z, Katy Perry cycle through the same performative loop just makes it clearer—this isn’t about art. It’s about staying on stage.
At this point, it’s less “celebrating creativity” and more method acting as meaning.
But hey—great news for “real people.”
At least tickets to the show are still free…
you just have to watch from the outside.

comments.text:
There was one woman with an amazing necklace with a huge stone of Tanzanite?  I'm not sure if I have the stone correct but her gown was embellished with the designs you would see in Indian architecture.  It was lovely.

But I have to tell you, there were some really unattractive gowns:  Katy Perry, Heidi Klum, Madonna,  Lena Dunham, just to name a few. 

I know Lauren Sanchez got slammed by the press, but I thought her gown was really clever for the theme.  It was the Sargent painting called Madame X that caused a scandal when he painted it because the dropped strap was considered slutty at the time.  That painting hangs in the Met, so it hit all the right notes and then was also a subtle acknowledgement of what people think of Lauren.  I got it right away because I'm familiar with the painting and the story.  I'm not a big fan of hers, but she definitely nailed the theme idea.  It's what I expected everyone else's dresses to be like, but some really went in a direction that didn't make any sense!
